note: Right picture: a B-tree/B+tree index stores the indexed values plus a pointer to the row, managed by the database. What the 'row ID' is depends on the engine. In InnoDB (MySQL 8.4) each secondary-index record holds the primary-key columns and InnoDB uses that value to look up the row in the clustered index. PostgreSQL indexes point to a physical tuple location instead.
Matches InnoDB (MySQL 8.4): each secondary-index record contains the indexed columns plus the primary-key columns, so with post_id as primary key an index on user_id holds (user_id, post_id).

MySQL 8.4 docs: every InnoDB secondary-index record carries the primary key, so 'if the primary key is long, the secondary indexes use more space, so it is advantageous to have a short primary key.' That is the UUID bloat argument.

Good heuristic stated as an absolute. Databases cache index and data pages as they are accessed and evict the least recently used ones (InnoDB buffer pool, MySQL 8.4). What has to fit in RAM is the hot working set of indexes and data, not every index in full. A database whose cold or rarely used index pages sit on disk can still be fast. Conversely, indexes fitting in RAM doesn't fix bad queries or missing indexes.
precise_version: For consistently fast queries, the frequently used part of your indexes (and hot data) should fit in the database's memory cache; if hot index pages keep getting read from disk, queries slow down sharply.

note: True for index-only (covering) plans, but not how every query runs. In PostgreSQL 'in an ordinary index scan, each row retrieval requires fetching data from both the index and the heap', with random heap access during execution, not only as a last step. Index-only scans need every referenced column to be in the index. Non-indexed filters, non-covering joins and sequential scans all read table rows mid-plan.
precise_version: The planner uses indexes to find matching rows cheaply; if the index covers every column the query needs it may never touch the table, otherwise it fetches table rows as it goes.

note: Holds for covering/index-only plans. Otherwise table rows are read during execution too. Those reads are often RAM hits as well, because the buffer pool caches table data as well as index pages (InnoDB, MySQL 8.4).

Teacher's personal practice and a sweeping 'in most cases'. No public source can confirm the frequency. Checking index size versus memory is a sound early step; slow-query logs and EXPLAIN plans (missing or unused indexes, bad queries) are the other usual first checks.

Index pages are loaded into memory on demand and cached, but they are not kept indefinitely. InnoDB caches table and index data as it is accessed and evicts least-recently-used pages when room is needed. At boot, MySQL 8.4 by default reloads only the most recently used 25% of pages, saved at the previous shutdown, not all indexes.

Same over-generalisation as L-0136. The memory cache must hold the hot working set; total index size is a rough upper bound for indexes alone. RAM also has to cover hot data pages, connections and the OS (MySQL docs: dedicated servers often give up to 80% of memory to the buffer pool). So 'RAM = index size' would actually be too little if every index were hot.
precise_version: Size the database's memory cache (e.g. InnoDB buffer pool) to hold the hot indexes and data; RAM must exceed that, since the cache is usually at most ~80% of RAM.

note: AUTO_INCREMENT works on any MySQL integer type. INT is 4 bytes (unsigned max 4,294,967,295) and BIGINT is 8 bytes; Flickr's ticket table itself uses bigint unsigned auto_increment. MySQL advises the smallest type that holds the maximum value you need. Once the type's upper limit is reached, the next insert fails.
Flickr's 2010 engineering post (historical) says GUIDs 'index badly in MySQL' and 'If you can't keep your indexes in memory, you can't keep your database fast.'

Rule of thumb from the teacher's experience. A more careful version sizes for the hot working set of indexes and data and leaves headroom: the buffer pool usually takes at most ~80% of RAM, so RAM must be larger than whatever you want cached.
Correct as stated for this context: stateless API tiers scale horizontally easily, the stateful database is the hard part.
Correct as stated for this context.

'Delete + insert = upsert' is loose. An upsert inserts or updates in place. INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE performs an UPDATE of the old row, and only REPLACE is delete-then-insert. The two are not the same: delete+insert sets unspecified columns back to defaults and fires DELETE triggers.
precise_version: A delete-then-insert in one transaction can be replaced by a single upsert statement (insert, or update the existing row if the key already exists).

note: Correct as stated for this context.
MySQL 8.4: if the row would cause a duplicate in a UNIQUE index or PRIMARY KEY, 'an UPDATE of the old row occurs.'

MySQL 8.4: REPLACE tries the insert, and on a duplicate-key error for a primary key or unique index it deletes the conflicting row and retries the insert. The docs note an engine may implement this as an update, with the same semantics.

The 32x figure is the teacher's own benchmark. No public source confirms it, and the gap depends on indexes, triggers and foreign keys. REPLACE does more work (delete plus insert), so 'slower' is plausible. But 'either works' is misleading: REPLACE sets any column not given to its default, fires DELETE and INSERT triggers, and gets a new AUTO_INCREMENT value. ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE keeps the row and changes only the listed columns. Flickr's ticket server relies on REPLACE's new-ID behaviour.
precise_version: REPLACE INTO deletes and re-inserts the row, so it is usually slower than INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE (the teacher measured ~32x on one setup) and it resets columns you don't supply; prefer ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE unless you want a fresh row.

note: Correct as stated for this context. For example, PostgreSQL docs: 'The rows skipped by an OFFSET clause still have to be computed inside the server; therefore a large OFFSET might be inefficient.'

The concept is right: Instagram used 'several thousand logical shards that are mapped in code to far fewer physical shards'. Instagram ran PostgreSQL, though, and each logical shard was a Postgres schema inside a database, not a separate CREATE DATABASE. The MySQL CREATE DATABASE picture is the teacher's illustration of the same idea.
Instagram IDs reserve 13 bits for the logical shard ID (2^13 = 8192 possible shards), and they ran several thousand logical shards on far fewer physical servers. '10 or 15' is the teacher's example.
Illustrative. In Instagram's PostgreSQL setup each logical shard was a schema (e.g. insta5), not a separate database. See L-0267.
Instagram: each logical shard (Postgres schema) contains the same tables, duplicated in every shard.
Correct as stated for this context. Schema changes must be applied to every logical shard; 8,000 is the ID-space maximum, Instagram ran several thousand.

Instagram rebalances by 'moving a set of logical shards from one database to another'. A dump-and-load is one way to do it, but moving a live shard also needs writes to that shard to be paused or replicated during the cut-over. The post doesn't say Instagram used SQL dumps.
Instagram post: they can start with a few database servers and scale out by moving logical shards to new ones, without re-bucketing data.
Matches Instagram's stated benefit: moving whole logical shards avoids re-bucketing data row by row.

True for PostgreSQL, where serial/identity columns are backed by sequence objects whose nextval is atomic across sessions. MySQL has no sequence objects: InnoDB keeps a per-table AUTO_INCREMENT counter, and there is no nextval to call outside an insert. 'Every database' is too broad, though the atomic-counter idea holds.

Student proposal corrected by the teacher. In Instagram's PostgreSQL function, nextval('insta5.table_id_seq') reads a sequence named table_id_seq in the schema insta5; it is neither a column nor a table.

Correct for PostgreSQL. CREATE TABLE with a serial column is equivalent to CREATE SEQUENCE tablename_colname_seq plus DEFAULT nextval(...). Instagram's next_id() calls an explicitly named per-table sequence.
Student proposal corrected by the teacher. In PostgreSQL a sequence is created implicitly only for serial/identity columns; otherwise you create sequences explicitly with any name.

True in PostgreSQL, where a table may have several serial/identity columns or column defaults using nextval. False in MySQL, the other database used in this lecture: 'There can be only one AUTO_INCREMENT column per table, it must be indexed' (MySQL 8.4).
precise_version: In PostgreSQL a table can have several sequence-backed columns; MySQL allows only one AUTO_INCREMENT column per table.

note: PostgreSQL docs: nextval is atomic; 'even if multiple sessions execute nextval concurrently, each will safely receive a distinct sequence value.'
Student proposal corrected by the teacher. Sequences are persisted by the database, and the teacher's correction stands.

Correct. MySQL 8.4 writes the auto-increment counter to the redo log and data dictionary so it survives restarts. PostgreSQL sequences are durable, with optional in-memory caching (CACHE). Both trade gaps for speed.
